tagline: The tech-delay filler that became League's Game 5 anthem.
headline: A four-day library track looped through Riot's 2012 Worlds outages and became the sound of League's deciding Game 5s.
summary: Danny McCarthy wrote Silver Scrapes in about four days as anonymous production music, and Riot's stream looped it for hours while network failures stalled the Season 2 World Championship in Los Angeles in October 2012. Fans never forgot the loop, and Riot turned the joke into a tradition: the track now plays before the deciding game of a best-of-five, and "Silver Scrapes" has become shorthand for Game 5 itself. Riot has since released a Warsongs remix (2016), a USC Trojan Marching Band version, an LPL version on traditional Chinese instruments and a full orchestral recording for Worlds 2025.

story.heading: Four days on a broken laptop
story.body:
*Silver Scrapes* was never meant to be famous. Danny McCarthy told LoL Esports that he started composing at 15 and that it took roughly a decade before anyone paid him for it. His first gig came from the production-music library Killer Tracks when he was about 22 or 23. He wrote *Silver Scrapes* in about four days, against a strict deadline and with no money, on a ten-year-old laptop. The screen was cracked, most of the keys didn't work, and by his account the USB ports would give you a shock.

Production music works like this: a composer delivers a track to a library, and it can end up in an ad, a TV show or a stream without anyone learning who wrote it. theScore esports reports that McCarthy uploaded the track to Killer Tracks, a pay-to-use library, and that Riot happened to be using the service in 2012. The original is a short electronic cue, just 1:56 long, and it is on streaming services today as *Silver Scrapes (As Featured In League of Legends Season 2 World Championship)*.

story.heading: Los Angeles, October 2012: the loop
story.body:
The Season 2 World Championship ran in Los Angeles from October 4 to 13, 2012, with a $2 million prize pool, the largest in esports at the time. The early rounds were played at L.A. Live. On October 6 the last quarterfinal, CLG Europe against Team WE, fell apart. The arena's network went down during the second game and took the Twitch stream with it, which forced a remake, and a later drop interrupted the deciding game. PCGamesN reported that the day was by then three and a half hours behind schedule. Riot postponed the rest of the match and both semifinals, citing "connectivity issues at our LA Live venue", and said the remaining games would be played at a "secured location". That turned out to be USC's Galen Center, on October 10. Taipei Assassins won the final there on October 13 in front of about 10,000 fans.

During the outages the stream sat on a static World Championship screen while one EDM track played on loop. Strafe reports that one break lasted nearly two hours. That track was *Silver Scrapes*. The event drew more than eight million viewers, the most for any esports event up to then, so the loop had an unusually large captive audience. The waiting turned into a shared joke, and the joke stuck.

story.heading: The composer finds out
story.body:
McCarthy learned what had happened from friends who played League. They told him his song had just played on League of Legends for something like two hours. He checked YouTube and found an upload of *Silver Scrapes* with around half a million views. At the time he didn't know what League of Legends was.

In April 2015 LoL Esports published a short documentary about him, *Spotlight: A Look Inside Silver Scrapes*. In it he says that since then he has been able to support himself without a nine-to-five job, and he credits League and its fans for part of that. The film also reveals that he gave his fiancée all of the song's royalties as a Valentine's Day gift. He had started playing League himself, though he admitted he was sticking to bot games.

story.heading: From punchline to Game 5 anthem
story.body:
Riot embraced the joke. Namuwiki dates the Game 5 use to 2015, and theScore esports reported in 2019 that Riot blasts *Silver Scrapes* at regional playoffs and international events whenever a series goes to a fifth game. An emergency filler became the sound of maximum tension. The name became shorthand too: fans, casters and reporters say a best-of-five has "gone to Silver Scrapes". During MSI 2023 Cloud9's account posted just "SILVER SCRAPES", a music-note emoji and the event hashtag. By Worlds 2025, Riot's own primer listed a "Silver Scrapes" next to Pentakills and Baron steals as an event that drops rewards to viewers.

Korea came to the tradition late. According to Namuwiki, Riot Korea's broadcasts only started playing the track for deciding games at the MSI 2021 final, after years of fans asking why they didn't. Korean streaming culture had already added its own ritual: slowly putting on sunglasses as the track starts. Namuwiki also singles out the 2016 final between SK Telecom T1 and Samsung Galaxy at Staples Center, the first Worlds final to go the full five games.

story.heading: Remixed, marched and re-imagined
story.body:
Riot also gave the song a home in its own catalogue. On January 14, 2016 it released *Warsongs*, a free bundle of 11 electronic remixes of League music by artists including Arty, Marshmello, Jauz, Vicetone and Mako. ProtoShredanoid's *Silver Scrapes* remix closes the album. Its video on the League of Legends channel shows a glowing crystal that flares and dims with the music, and the remix is the version League's YouTube Music art track carries today. It has never been the main draw: at about 2.8 million views it is the second-least-watched of the 11 *Warsongs* videos, far behind *Piercing Light* at about 92.7 million. The song lives on the broadcast more than in playlists.

Other versions followed. Riot's 2018 College Championship promo used *Silver Scrapes (USC Trojan Marching Band)* as its soundtrack, and theScore reports that Riot made the marching-band version the login music for its collegiate championships. That ties the song back to USC, the university that owns the Galen Center where the Season 2 event finished. In June 2023 China's LPL released a Dragon Boat Festival version played on traditional Chinese instruments by the Ancient Music Orchestra of XAIU.

story.heading: Worlds 2025: the orchestra plays Game 5
story.body:
Thirteen years after the outages, LoL Esports gave the song a full orchestral treatment. *Silver Scrapes – Orchestral Theme* came out on October 28, 2025, the first day of the Worlds 2025 Knockout Stage. Its description opens: "If it's Game 5… it's gotta be Silver Scrapes." The Hungarian Studio Orchestra recorded it at the Italian Institute in Budapest under conductor Krisztian Balassa, with three vocalists and taiko drums. The credits name Danny McCarthy and Patrick Cunningham as writers of the original song, and the joke carries into them: the "lyrics" are listed as wordless syllables like "BUH DUH DUH". The video has passed 1.4 million views in under a year.

Twelve days after the release, the Worlds 2025 final in Chengdu went to Silver Scrapes. KT Rolster led T1 2-1, T1 forced a fifth game, then won it to complete a third straight world title. A track that once filled dead air on a broken broadcast now announces the most important game of the year.

whyItMatters: It is League esports' best-known accident: a production-library cue looped during the Season 2 Worlds network failures became a shared memory for the game's fans.
Riot turned the joke into a tradition. The track plays when a best-of-five reaches a deciding fifth game, at regional playoffs and international events alike.
Its name became part of League's vocabulary. "Silver Scrapes" means Game 5, and Riot's Worlds 2025 primer lists it as an event that triggers viewer drops.
The tradition crossed regions, from Korean broadcasts and the Korean sunglasses ritual to an LPL version played on traditional Chinese instruments.

Riot keeps re-releasing it: a Warsongs remix (2016), a USC Trojan Marching Band version for the College Championship, and a Budapest orchestral recording for Worlds 2025 that has passed 1.4M YouTube views.
It changed its composer's life. Danny McCarthy says League's fans helped him make a living from music, and LoL Esports made a documentary about him.

communityMoments.title: The day the connection died
communityMoments.description: Repeated network crashes at L.A. Live wrecked the CLG Europe vs. Team WE quarterfinal and left the day three and a half hours behind schedule. Riot postponed the deciding game and both semifinals and moved them to a "secured location", which turned out to be USC's Galen Center.

communityMoments.title: Silver Scrapes on loop
communityMoments.description: During the Season 2 Worlds downtime the stream showed a static World Championship screen while Silver Scrapes looped. Strafe reports one break of nearly two hours, and the song became the event's unofficial anthem.

communityMoments.title: Riot puts the composer in the spotlight
communityMoments.description: LoL Esports published a mini-documentary about Danny McCarthy. It covers writing the song on a cracked ten-year-old laptop, hearing it had played on League for two hours, and giving its royalties to his fiancée.

communityMoments.title: Warsongs makes it official
communityMoments.description: Riot's free Warsongs remix album closed with ProtoShredanoid's take on Silver Scrapes, alongside remixes by Arty, Marshmello, Jauz and Mako.

communityMoments.title: The first five-game Worlds final
communityMoments.description: SK Telecom T1 beat Samsung Galaxy 3-2 at Staples Center in Los Angeles, the first Worlds final to go the full five games. Namuwiki's article on Silver Scrapes features the 2-2 moment.

communityMoments.title: The USC Trojan Marching Band version
communityMoments.description: Riot's 2018 College Championship promo used Silver Scrapes (USC Trojan Marching Band) as its soundtrack, a version recorded by the band of the university whose Galen Center hosted the Season 2 final.

communityMoments.title: Korea's broadcast joins in
communityMoments.description: According to Namuwiki, Riot Korea's broadcasts first played Silver Scrapes for a deciding game at the MSI 2021 final, RNG's 3-2 win over DWG KIA, which settled the Game 5 tradition in Korea.

communityMoments.title: The sunglasses ritual
communityMoments.description: In Korea, slowly putting on sunglasses as Silver Scrapes starts became a streamer meme. Namuwiki traces it to former pro gamer Ahn Ki-hyo, and Twitch chats answer Game 5s with sunglasses-cat emotes.

communityMoments.title: "SILVER SCRAPES"
communityMoments.description: Team accounts joined in too: during MSI 2023, Cloud9 posted "SILVER SCRAPES" with a music-note emoji and the #MSI2023 tag.

communityMoments.title: A Dragon Boat Festival version
communityMoments.description: The LPL released a special version of Silver Scrapes performed on traditional Chinese instruments by the Ancient Music Orchestra of XAIU.

communityMoments.title: Silver Scrapes earns viewers drops
communityMoments.description: Riot's Worlds 2025 primer said viewers could earn an Esports 2025 Capsule whenever a Pentakill, Baron steal, Dragon steal or Silver Scrapes happened.

communityMoments.title: The orchestra takes Game 5
communityMoments.description: LoL Esports released Silver Scrapes – Orchestral Theme, recorded by the Hungarian Studio Orchestra in Budapest, on the first day of the Worlds 2025 Knockout Stage.

communityMoments.title: A three-peat decided at Silver Scrapes
communityMoments.description: KT Rolster led the Worlds 2025 final 2-1, but T1 forced a fifth game and won it in Chengdu for a third straight title.

keyMoments.label: The crystal wakes
keyMoments.description: A dark crystal in a mechanical cradle fades in on a black ridge, then bursts into blue-white light about two seconds in.

keyMoments.label: Full power
keyMoments.description: The track reaches full volume and the crystal's glow starts strobing in time with it.

keyMoments.label: Flare
keyMoments.description: The crystal erupts in a burst of light and sparks, starting the video's brightest stretch.

keyMoments.label: Lights out
keyMoments.description: The breakdown: the music drops back and the crystal goes dark, with only green energy flickering around its edges.

keyMoments.label: Re-ignition
keyMoments.description: The volume comes back up and the crystal reignites in a shower of sparks.

keyMoments.label: One more fake-out
keyMoments.description: The crystal dims again for a few seconds before flaring back to life around 2:48.

keyMoments.label: Fade to black
keyMoments.description: The music winds down and the crystal slowly fades into darkness.

keyMoments.label: Four days, one broken laptop
keyMoments.description: McCarthy explains he wrote Silver Scrapes in about four days, broke, on a ten-year-old laptop with a cracked screen.

keyMoments.label: The Worlds 2012 loop
keyMoments.description: He recalls Riot's technical errors at Worlds 2012, his song playing on an hours-long loop, and friends telling him it had been on League for two hours.

keyMoments.label: A gift of royalties
keyMoments.description: McCarthy introduces his fiancée, who then describes the Valentine's Day letter in which he gave her all of the song's royalties.

featuredClip.description: After the breakdown the crystal sits dark with green energy curling around it, then reignites at about 2:13 in a blue-white flash and keeps pulsing as sparks drift past.
